I believe they are guaranteed to be present, as per [their entry in the official LSP spec page](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#diagnosticRelatedInformation):
> `DiagnosticRelatedInformation` is defined as follows:
> ```ts
> /**
>  * Represents a related message and source code location for a diagnostic.
>  * This should be used to point to code locations that cause or are related to
>  * a diagnostics, e.g when duplicating a symbol in a scope.
>  */
> export interface DiagnosticRelatedInformation {
> 	/**
> 	 * The location of this related diagnostic information.
> 	 */
> 	location: Location;
> 
> 	/**
> 	 * The message of this related diagnostic information.
> 	 */
> 	message: string;
> }
> ```

The `location` and `message` attributes aren't marked as nullable/optional, whereas other attributes sometimes are. For example, `Command.attributes` a little ways down the page:
> ```ts
> interface Command {
>	/**
>	 * Title of the command, like `save`.
>	 */
>	title: string;
>	/**
>	 * The identifier of the actual command handler.
>	 */
>	command: string;
>	/**
>	 * Arguments that the command handler should be
>	 * invoked with.
>	 */
>	arguments?: LSPAny[]; // <-- It has the ?, indicating it is optional(?)
> }
> ```

Following this logic, I may need to go through and double-check that any of the other LSP structures I added respect particular values being optional.

| IDE           | Shortcut               | Taken by Godot                                        |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Eclipse       | Cmd + 1                | Spatial Editor > 1 Viewport                           |
| Notepad++     | None                   | n/a                                                   |

| Rider         | Ctrl + Alt + Shift + T | No                                                    |
| Sublime Text  | None                   | n/a                                                   |
| VS Code       | Cmd + .                | Stop Running Project                                  |
| Visual Studio | Cmd + . or Alt + Enter | Stop Running Project or Common > UI Toggle Fullscreen |
| Xcode         | Cmd + '                | Canvas Item Editor > Toggle Grid                      |
| Zed           | Cmd + .                | Stop Running Project                                  |

(Note that these are Mac shortcuts; for Windows, replace Cmd with Ctrl)

This probably applies to some other remove actions too.

Unused variables can be assigned and still be unused, so any of those references won't be removed when the declaration is removed. It causes them to be an undeclared identifier error.

```gdscript
var unused = 1
unused = 2
```

Not sure if this can be fixed to delete all assignments too. Especially because it could be multi-document.
Thanks for catching this! I've updated the code to use the full range of the node, so that it deletes the whole declaration for variables, class variables, and constants.

That's a good point that hadn't occurred to me before. I'm feeling inclined to just remove this code action from the PR. Even if there was a way to fix it to delete all assignments, I could see the possibility of it causing cascading errors if the variable is, for example, assigned the result of a function with side effects:
```gdscript

var health = 5

func take_damage():
  health -= 1
  return health

func _on_hit():
  var unused = 1
  unused = take_damage()
  print("new health is %s" % health)
```
This is a bit of a silly quick example, but hopefully the issue is still visible: If the code action removes `unused`'s assignment line, then the behavior of the overall program will be changed.

If you think it'd be best to just remove those code actions for now, I can get that done. The class variables and constants may also need it removed, as they can be assigned the results of functions with side effects too.

The action does only say it will remove the *declaration*, so I think it is probably fine to keep it. It is still useful in common scenarios. 
And if the declaration has side effects, it is up to the user to decide to remove it or take another action for the warning.
